title: Game Changer: Unpacking India's Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026 After Presidential Assent
content:
# Game Changer: Unpacking India's Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026 After Presidential Assent "Tax laws are like a river, always flowing and adapting to the economic landscape." As professionals, we know this all too well, constantly navigating the currents of regulatory change. The recent Presidential Assent to the **Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026**, on August 17, 2026, marks another significant bend in this river, bringing with it crucial adjustments that demand our immediate attention and a thorough understanding. This isn't just another amendment; it's a strategic move by the government to bolster economic growth, attract foreign investment, and streamline critical digital infrastructure and payment systems. Let’s dive deep into what this new Act means for businesses, investors, and us, the torchbearers of compliance. ## The Genesis of the Change: From Ordinance to Act Before becoming a full-fledged Act, many of these provisions were initially introduced through the **Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026**, promulgated on June 5, 2026. Ordinances are temporary legislative measures, and it's always critical for their provisions to be ratified by Parliament to gain permanency. The passage of the Bill by Parliament on August 10, 2026, and subsequent Presidential Assent, solidifies these changes, ensuring continuity and legal certainty. Importantly, actions already taken under the Ordinance will remain valid and will be treated as if taken under the corresponding provisions of this new Act. This transition from Ordinance to Act demonstrates the government's commitment to these reforms, addressing evolving geopolitical developments and aiming to mitigate external economic shocks. This comprehensive Act primarily amends the **Income-tax Act, 2025**, the **Finance Act, 2026**, and the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. Its stated objectives are broad: to attract more foreign capital, promote domestic electronics manufacturing, and provide "process certainty" for foreign cloud companies utilizing Indian data centres. Additionally, it aims to deepen the Government Securities (G-Secs) market and enhance Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) participation. ## Direct Tax Amendments: A Closer Look The direct tax provisions introduced by this Act are designed to be a catalyst for economic activity, particularly in attracting foreign investment and boosting domestic manufacturing. ### 1. Relief for Foreign Investors in Government Securities (G-Secs) One of the standout provisions is the tax exemption for Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on income from government securities. This is a significant policy shift aimed at making India's G-Sec market more attractive globally. | Old Provision (Pre-Amendment) | New Provision (Post-Amendment) | | :------------------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Interest income from G-Secs was taxed at 20%. | Exempt from income tax. | | Short-term capital gains from G-Secs were taxed at 30%. | Exempt from income tax. | | Long-term capital gains from G-Secs were taxed at 12.5%. | Exempt from income tax. | | *Applicability:* These changes apply to income arising on or after April 1, 2026. | *Impact:* This move significantly reduces the tax burden for major foreign players, potentially leading to increased inflows into India's government bond market, strengthening the rupee and providing easier access to funds for government projects. It removes a notable hurdle for foreign portfolio investors. | ### 2. Easing the Path for Foreign Fund Managers Relocating to India The Act also streamlines the framework for investment funds registered outside India but managed from India. Earlier, such funds faced a plethora of conditions to avoid their global income being taxed in India due to a perceived "business connection." Now, a significant number of these conditions have been removed. | Old Provision (Pre-Amendment) | New Provision (Post-Amendment) | | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Funds had to satisfy multiple conditions, including:
* A minimum of 25 members.
* Maximum 10% participation interest for a single investor.
* Minimum monthly average corpus requirement of ₹100 crore.
* A bar on investing more than 25% of the corpus in a single entity. | Several of these onerous conditions have been deleted. This simplifies the compliance landscape substantially.
*Impact:* This rationalisation aims to make India a more attractive destination for managing global investment funds, potentially leading to the relocation of fund managers and creation of high-value jobs within the financial sector in India. It signals a clear intent to cut down on bureaucratic hurdles and promote ease of doing business for global financial entities. Foreign funds using Indian fund managers are still required to maintain records covering investor composition, corpus, Indian participation, fund-manager contributions, and registration status, submitting a prescribed statement within 90 days from the end of the tax year. | ### 3. Boosting Domestic Electronics Manufacturing In a significant push for the 'Make in India' initiative, the Act extends crucial tax exemptions for the electronics manufacturing sector. This targets foreign companies involved in contract manufacturing within India. * **Extended Exemption:** Income tax exemption for foreign companies engaging contract manufacturers in India for producing electronic goods has been extended until **2040-41**. This provides long-term policy certainty, a crucial factor for large-scale investments. * **Bonded Warehouse Benefits:** Furthermore, the Act introduces an income exemption for foreign companies that store components in a customs bonded warehouse in India, provided these components are supplied to contract manufacturers of specified electronic goods (e.g., phones, laptops, servers). This exemption is applicable for income arising on or after October 1, 2026, and is available until March 31, 2041. This move is expected to streamline supply chains and reduce costs for electronics manufacturers, making India a more competitive manufacturing hub. ### 4. Clarity and Incentives for Data Centres Recognising the growing importance of digital infrastructure, the Act also clarifies and expands the tax benefits related to data centres. * The definition of a "specified data centre" under Schedule IV of the Income Tax Act 2025 has been amended. * Previously, exemptions for services procured from data centres had specific conditions, including the foreign company being notified by the central government and the data centre being part of an approved scheme. * The new Act removes these stringent notification requirements and extends the exemption to services procured from data centres that are **leased and operated by an Indian company**, not just those owned and operated by them. A specified data centre must now be operated by an Indian company, either by owning or leasing it, and must satisfy other prescribed conditions. This broadening of scope provides much-needed flexibility and incentives for the expansion of data centre infrastructure in India, which is vital for the digital economy. ### 5. Rationalisation for Business Trusts (REITs & InvITs) The Act also brings about important changes concerning business trusts, such as Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs). * **Surcharge Adjustment:** For Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) of business trusts that opt for concessional tax regimes, the surcharge rate has been raised to **25%**. * **Dividend Income Exemption:** Crucially, unit holders of a business trust will now be exempt from tax on income representing dividends from such an SPV, irrespective of the tax regime chosen by the underlying SPV. This aims to streamline the taxation of dividend distributions and offer a more predictable tax environment for investors in business trusts. ## Beyond Taxation: Amendments to Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 While the primary focus is on taxation, the Act also brings a significant amendment to the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. This change has direct implications for digital payments, especially UPI and RuPay transactions. * **Legal Backing for MDR Changes:** The Act now provides legal backing to the government to modify the **zero-MDR (Merchant Discount Rate)** framework for UPI and RuPay card transactions. This means the government can, by notification, determine which electronic payment modes or transactions will remain free from MDR charges. * **Consumer Assurance:** Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has clarified that UPI payments will continue to be free for consumers. Any future MDR, if introduced, would apply only to specific categories of merchant transactions. The UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI, will now be instrumental in deciding these MDR charges. This amendment is a critical step towards creating a sustainable model for digital payments while balancing the interests of consumers, merchants, and payment service providers. ## A Broader Perspective: Why These Changes Matter This Act is more than just a collection of tax tweaks; it reflects a strategic vision for India's economic future. By making it easier for foreign capital to flow into G-Secs, simplifying conditions for offshore fund management, and extending long-term incentives for electronics manufacturing and data centres, the government is signalling its intent to integrate India more deeply into the global economy. The changes to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act also highlight a proactive approach to managing the growth and sustainability of India's digital public infrastructure. For professionals, yeh ek naya chapter hai jismein humein apni expertise aur advisory skills ko aur sharpen karna hoga. ## Final Thoughts The **Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026**, receiving Presidential Assent, marks a pivotal moment for India's economic policy. The amendments are largely growth-oriented, focusing on attracting foreign investment, fostering domestic manufacturing, and strengthening digital infrastructure. As Chartered Accountants and Legal Analysts, our role becomes even more critical in interpreting these changes, advising clients on their implications, and ensuring seamless compliance. The devil, as always, will be in the details of the official notifications and circulars that follow. So, stay vigilant, stay informed! ## Read the Official Document * [Download the Official Notification/Circular here](https://egazette.nic.in/) *Published on: 23 August 2026*
